AND LINDA J. BURGESS ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES (ALJs), STATE OFFICE OF

ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS (SOAH):

        COMES NOW, G-9 and G-13 Landowners and files this Reply Brief in the above-styled

and numbered docket. In support thereof, G-9 and G-13 Landowners1 shows the following:

                                        I.     INTRODUCTION

        Since June 12, 2026, the last day of the hearing on the merits, parties participating in this

proceeding have filed a total of 130 initial briefs. For purposes of this Reply Brief, these briefs

are divided into 3 categories: (1) those supportive of Route 296, (2) those unopposed to Route 296,

and (3) those opposed to Route 296. In total, 121 briefs fall into these categories. The remaining




        1
           The G-9 and G-13 Landowners include Jeff Kubin acting in the interest of The Highgate West Group LLC
(d/b/a The Highgate Group LLC) (owners of tract 2141), Bob Guthrie acting in the interest of Guthrie Ranching LTD
(owners of tracts 2127 and 2128), and James Giddens acting in the interest of JKME Family Limited Partnership
(owners of tracts 2147 and 5142).

                                                       2
 9 briefs oppose the Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA

Transmission Service Corporation (collectively, Applicants) entirely.

         Of the 121 briefs, 76 either support or are unopposed to Route 296 based on express

language or the link they are affected by. These intervenors constitute almost two-thirds of the

participating intervenors in this case. Conversely, 45 intervenors, or 37%, either directly opposed

Route 296 or opposed links that are on Route 296. However, many of the opposing intervenors’

briefs consist of only generalized criticisms of the impact of the transmission line on their property.

Specific criticisms include the proximity of Florence Elementary School on Link F34, potential

expansion of a pipeline, and route performance based on objective criteria in the Public Utility

Regulatory Act (PURA) and the Public Utility Commission of Texas’ (PUC) Rules. Although

these concerns are relevant, none of them alter the overall position of Route 296 as the best meets

route.

         PURA and the Commission Rules lay out multiple factors that must be taken into

consideration when selecting a “best meets route.” Major issues related to these factors arose

during the hearing and were addressed in the parties’ initial briefs. Included in these issues were

concerns regarding the environmental integrity of the selected route as it crosses the Colorado

River and runs nearby state parks, engineering constraints related to proposed infrastructure

expansion and flooding, and community values. Each of these concerns are addressed in detail

below. As the record demonstrates, Route 296 is a superior route that should be selected as best

meets route. It not only meets the criteria set out in PURA and Commission Rules, but it also

alleviates the concerns of the majority of intervenors.




                                                  3
      II.     ROUTE 296 SHOULD BE SELECTED AS THE BEST MEETS ROUTE

       Objectively, with respect to the criteria set forth in PURA and Commission Rules, Route

296 performs as well as or better than other routes of interest including Routes 487 and 894. The

cost estimate for Route 296 is $1,684,563,000. This is comparable to the least expensive route,

$1,636,232,000.2 Route 296 also is estimated to cost just 1% more than Routes 8943 and 4874.

Additionally, Route 296 crosses less riparian areas than Routes 894 or 487. Route 296 crosses no

upland woodlands and follows more compatible rights-of-way than Routes 894 and 487. Although

Route 296 is located closer to more habitable structures (nine more than Route 487 over 223 miles

and 20 more than Route 894 over the same distance), there are 126 separate intervenors on 14 links

directly impacted by Route 894 or 487 that will be spared if Route 296 were selected. Additionally,

Route 296 avoids Link E6, which was highlighted for having the most habitable structures located

on a proposed link.

       In addition to the objective criteria, Route 296 is a superior route as it alleviates intervenors’

concerns related to the environmental integrity of crossing the Colorado River and going nearby

multiple state parks, engineering constraints related to proposed infrastructure expansion and

flooding, and community values.

 A. Environmental Integrity

        1. Link J31 is the Superior Route to Cross the Colorado River

        Pursuant to PURA5 and Commission Rules6 one of the factors taken into consideration by

the Commission in selecting a route is environmental integrity. It is imperative to maintain the

environmental integrity of the study area by selecting a route that minimally impacts the Colorado

River and nearby state parks: Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park. All routes

cross the Colorado River using one of the following links: U3, U2, J11, J26, J22, or J31.

        Despite expressed concerns regarding each of the five links crossing the Colorado River,

the evidence is clear that Link J31 is the best option. Nevertheless, the Colorado River Alliance

Intervenors and G6 Landowners Legal Fund, LLC assert that Link J31 is inferior because it runs

nearly parallel to a pipeline that crosses the Colorado River underground.7 This concern relates to

the interaction of the pipeline and the transmission line. As also noted by the Colorado River

Alliance Intervenors, there is a way to mitigate these impacts by using cathodic protection.8

Although this may increase the costs of routes using Link J31, Applicants’ witness, Coring Cooley,

confirmed that the cost estimates for the proposed transmission line include a 10-15%

contingency.9 Thus, this mitigation effort could fall within the 10-15% contingency included in

the cost estimate. Moreover, paralleling a pipeline should not be a determinative factor. Not only

do Applicants admit that such option should be reasonably considered,10 but, as highlighted by

pipeline rights-of-way.11

        The crossing of the Colorado River at Link J31, and traversing near an established right-

of-way, is preferred as it will avoid disrupting pristine portions along the Colorado River.

Applicants’ witness, Mr. Marusak, affirmed this at the hearing by asserting that when crossing a

river, it is preferable to utilize existing corridors that have already been disrupted.12 Unlike Link

J31, Link J22 does not use an existing right-of-way, is located near Post Oak Ridge State Park,

and would disrupt visitors’ enjoyment of the Park due to the visibility of the transmission line from

the Park. Similarly, Link J26 would be within the foreground visible zone from the Post Oak

Ridge State Park and Link J11 would be within the foreground visual zone of Colorado Bend State

Park. Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, Texas State Parks Division, conducted a viewshed

analysis and noted that “[a] 150-200-foot-tall transmission line and tower within 5 miles of a scenic

viewpoint valued for its natural qualities, is likely to be distracting to most visitors. The distance

within the foreground middle ground where form, line, color, and texture contrasts are most

apparent to the casual observer.”13 As Links J22, J26, and J11 are closer to the parks than 5 miles,

they will be visible and distracting to visitors.

        When compared to Links U2 and U3 which cross the Colorado River further north, Link

J31 better preserves the environmental integrity of the study area. When looking at the number of

streams crossed by the links and the length of the links across riparian areas, Link J31 performs

crosses 19.14 Furthermore, Link J31 traverses through 4.62 miles of riparian areas while Link U2

traverses through 7.24 miles and Link U3 traverses through 8.16 miles of riparian areas.15

       For these reasons, Link J31 is the superior link to use when crossing the Colorado River as

it preserves the environmental integrity and protects the visual integrity of both Colorado Bend

State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park.

       2. Route 296 Avoids the Hidden Springs Preserve

       Located just south of Link G9, is the Hidden Springs Ranch Preserve (Preserve). As noted

by Applicants, the Preserve is 633.9 acres of property established for golden-cheeked warbler

conservation.16 The Preserve is owned by the Williamson County Conservation Foundation.

Approved members who have completed training sessions and members of the public are allowed

on the Preserve to conduct biological surveys and monitoring.17 As noted by the M31, M32, and

M33 Landowners, Link G9 runs within 1,000 feet of the Preserve for about 1.63 miles.18 Although

the Preserve is not a Texas Parks and Wildlife Department owned property, standards set by Texas

Parks and Wildlife Department should be applicable as preservation of the preserve is as important

to the environmental integrity of the area as a state park. Taking this into consideration, Texas

Parks and Wildlife Department recommends that transmission lines should avoid “ridgelines and

hilltops near TPWD properties of interest.”19 Link G9 directly conflicts with this recommendation.

        As the illustration shows, at least one structure of the proposed transmission line would be

visible from almost anywhere in the Preserve.24 Allowing a transmission structure to run so close

to, and visible from, the Preserve would diminish the conservation efforts the Preserve was created

for. For this reason, routes using Link G9 should be avoided in order to maintain the environmental

integrity of the Preserve. Route 296 does not use Link G9 and should be chosen as best meets

route to avoid disrupting the conservation efforts at the Preserve.

B. Engineering Constraints

       Several intervenors raise a variety of concerns in their briefs pertaining to engineering

constraints, including concerns regarding flooding in the area and an expansion of a pipeline

compressor station.

       For example, the Yates Keith Alliance Intervenors’ Initial Brief discusses the expansion of

the Matterhorn Pipeline Compressor Station as a potential engineering constraint.25                       The

Matterhorn Pipeline Compressor Station is located near Link G31, which is a link on Route 296.

Yates Keith Alliance Intervenors makes this assertion by relying on a line of questioning that

occurred during the hearing between Susan Warren, a G1 Landowner and spokesperson, and

Applicants’ witnesses, Mr. Marusak and Ms. Cooley.26 Yates Keith Alliance picks specific

portions of this discussion and leaves out important details. For starters, when Mr. Marusak noted

that “we can agree that G31, as proposed, would cross that, you know, planned expansion” 27 Mr.

Marusak was not looking at a specific expansion plan, but instead was looking at a screen that

showed the Applicants’ constraint map with a cursor controlled by Ms. Warren in an attempt to

C. Community Values

       1. Participation in Proceeding

       As described in PURA and Commission Rules, community value is one of the factors the

Commission must take into consideration when determining the best meets route. Community

values are often determined through the participation of community members in a transmission

line proceeding.       In addition to community values, habitable structures are also taken into

consideration.35 Despite this, Jerome and Gaylynn Sneed assert that “the habitable structures

whose owners do not file comments or evidence opposing the CCN should not factor into the

analysis of habitable structures for routing purposes.”36 In making this assertion, the Sneed’s

adjust the Applicants’ habitable structure count between Routes 891 (the Sneeds’ proposed route

which was not included in Applicants’ 122 alternative routes), 296, and 894 to show only those

habitable structures whose owners intervened.37 Specifically, Route 891, which Applicants’ show

having 108 habitable structures, was adjusted to only 46 habitable structures that opposed the

Route. Similarly, Route 296 went from 105 habitable structures to 33 habitable structures that

opposed that Route, and Route 894 decreased from 85 habitable structures to 44.38 This logic is

flawed and should not be taken into consideration. When looking at the habitable structure count,

all habitable structures that would be affected should be taken into consideration.       While

participation of parties in opposition of a proposed route can be informative with respect to

 community values, it should not be determinative of the number of habitable structures that would

be affected by the transmission line. That would pose an unfair expectation on unrepresented, and

potentially unaware, landowners.

        Instead, with respect to habitable structures, what should be evaluated is the location of

those structures and the resulting impact. The habitable structures that will feel the most significant

impact from these transmission lines are those within 200 feet. Those landowners will not only

have a transmission line outside their front door, but they will be closer to the noise emitted from

the lines, will be in close proximity to construction and maintenance of the transmission line, and

some may even be at risk if the transmission lines were to fall. Looking specifically at those

habitable structures, despite having more habitable structures within 500 feet than Routes 894 and

487, Route 296 has the same amount of habitable structures within 200 feet as Routes 894 and

487. Because of those homes within such proximity, the severe impact of Routes 296, 894, and

487 on habitable structures are the same. An example of a close habitable structure that would be

included on Routes 894 and 487 is owned by Aaron Games and his family, which consists of his

wife and their children. As proposed, Link G13 will be just 175 feet from the Games’ family

home.39 This close proximity will not only impact the aesthetic value of the property, but it will

also massively diminish the value of the property financially and the enjoyment of the property,

as well as create a nuisance that will ensue for the Games family who inhabit their home daily as

construction and maintenance on the transmission line will be a continuous occurrence.40

        While homes within 200 feet are severely impacted by the transmission lines, there are

homes just outside of the 500-foot benchmark for consideration of “affected habitable structures”

         2. Link F34

        Another concern that was brought up in briefs was the proximity of Florence Elementary

School to Link F34 which is included on Route 296. In particular, general concerns were raised

about having a line in the proximity of the school. The Colorado River Alliance Intervenors state

that “after learning that fact, Commission Staff confirmed that Route 296 is an ‘inappropriate

route.’”48 However, this statement is false. In its brief, Commission Staff asserts that “[e]xcept

for noting that Mr. Poole would encourage the Commission against approving any route that uses

Segment E6, Staff does not contest the viability of any of proposed routes.”49 As Commission

Staff asserts, it does not contest the viability of any proposed routes, including those that include

Link F34.

        Despite some intervenors’ contention that routes using Link F34 should be disqualified,50

modifications can be made to address the concern regarding the proximity of the school if Link F34

is adopted. Despite Applicants’ contention that there should be no health effects as the closest

boundary of the school is nearly 400 feet away,51 caution is still warranted and impacts on the

school should be further mitigated. As asserted previously in the G-9 and G-13 Landowners’

Initial Brief, Applicants should mitigate intervenors’ concerns and the impact to the school by

making modifications to add distance between the transmission line and the school. Further,

Tract 2361, located north of the school, appears to be undeveloped and the landowner is not a

participant in the current proceeding. Thus, the transmission line could potentially be moved

further away from the school and closer to Tract 2361 to mitigate impacts. For this reason,

 Route 296 should not be “disqualified” and, instead, Applicants should be required to work with

                                  III.    CONCLUSION

       For the reasons stated herein, and in the G-9 and G-13 Landowners’ Initial Brief, the G-9

and G-13 Landowners respectfully request the Administrative Law Judges recommend selection

of Route 296 to the Commission as the best meets route. The G-9 and G-13 Landowners

additionally request any other relief to which they have shown themselves entitled.

         PURA and the Commission Rules lay out multiple factors that must be taken into

consideration when selecting a "best meets route." Major issues related to these factors arose

during the hearing and were addressed in the parties' initial briefs. Included in these issues were

concerns regarding the environmental integrity of the selected route as it crosses the Colorado

River and runs nearby state parks, engineering constraints related to proposed infrastructure

expansion and flooding, and community values. Each of these concerns are addressed in detail

below. As the record demonstrates, Route 296 is a superior route that should be selected as best

meets route. It not only meets the criteria set out in PURA and Commission Rules, but it also

alleviates the concerns of the maj ority of intervenors.

      II.    ROUTE 296 SHOULD BE SELECTED AS THE BEST MEETS ROUTE

        Objectively, with respect to the criteria set forth in PURA and Commission Rules, Route

296 performs as well as or better than other routes of interest including Routes 487 and 894. The

cost estimate for Route 296 is $ 1 , 684 , 563 , 000 . This is comparable to the least expensive route ,

$1,636,232,000.2 Route 296 also is estimated to cost just 1% more than Routes 8943 and 4874

Additionally, Route 296 crosses less riparian areas than Routes 894 or 487. Route 296 crosses no

upland woodlands and follows more compatible rights-of-way than Routes 894 and 487. Although

Route 296 is located closer to more habitable structures (nine more than Route 487 over 223 miles

and 20 more than Route 894 over the same distance), there are 126 separate intervenors on 14 links

directly impacted by Route 894 or 487 that will be spared ifRoute 296 were selected. Additionally,

Route 296 avoids Link E6, which was highlighted for having the most habitable structures located

on a proposed link.

       In addition to the objective criteria, Route 296 is a superior route as it alleviates intervenors'

concerns related to the environmental integrity of crossing the Colorado River and going nearby

multiple state parks, engineering constraints related to proposed infrastructure expansion and

flooding, and community values.

 A. Environmental Integrity

        1. Link J31 is the Superior Route to Cross the Colorado River

        Pursuant to PURA5 and Commission Rules6 one of the factors taken into consideration by

the Commission in selecting a route is environmental integrity. It is imperative to maintain the

environmental integrity of the study area by selecting a route that minimally impacts the Colorado

River and nearby state parks: Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park. All routes

cross the Colorado River using one of the following links: U3, U2, Jll, J26, J22, or J31.

        Despite expressed concerns regarding each of the five links crossing the Colorado River,

the evidence is clear that Link J31 is the best option. Nevertheless, the Colorado River Alliance

Intervenors and G6 Landowners Legal Fund, LLC assert that Link J31 is inferior because it runs

nearly parallel to a pipeline that crosses the Colorado River underground.7 This concern relates to

the interaction of the pipeline and the transmission line. As also noted by the Colorado River

Alliance Intervenors, there is a way to mitigate these impacts by using cathodic protection.8

Although this may increase the costs of routes using Link J31, Applicants' witness, Coring Cooley,

confirmed that the cost estimates for the proposed transmission line include a 10-15%

contingency.' Thus, this mitigation effort could fall within the 10-15% contingency included in

the cost estimate. Moreover, paralleling a pipeline should not be a determinative factor. Not only

do Applicants admit that such option should be reasonably considered, 10 but, as highlighted by

C. Community Values

       1. Participation in Proceeding

       As described in PURA and Commission Rules, community value is one of the factors the

Commission must take into consideration when determining the best meets route. Community

values are often determined through the participation of community members in a transmission

line proceeding.     In addition to community values, habitable structures are also taken into

consideration.35 Despite this, Jerome and Gaylynn Sneed assert that "the habitable structures

whose owners do not file comments or evidence opposing the CCN should not factor into the

analysis of habitable structures for routing purposes."36 In making this assertion, the Sneed's

adjust the Applicants' habitable structure count between Routes 891 (the Sneeds' proposed route

which was not included in Applicants' 122 alternative routes), 296, and 894 to show only those

habitable structures whose owners intervened.37 Specifically, Route 891, which Applicants' show

having 108 habitable structures, was adjusted to only 46 habitable structures that opposed the

Route. Similarly, Route 296 went from 105 habitable structures to 33 habitable structures that

opposed that Route, and Route 894 decreased from 85 habitable structures to 44.38 This logic is

flawed and should not be taken into consideration. When looking at the habitable structure count,

Wl habitable structures that would be affected should be taken into consideration.         While

participation of parties in opposition of a proposed route can be informative with respect to

         2. Link F34

        Another concern that was brought up in briefs was the proximity of Florence Elementary

School to Link F34 which is included on Route 296. In particular, general concerns were raised

route. „,48 However, this statement is false. In its brief, Commission Staff asserts that "[elxcept

Segment E6, Staff does not contest the viability of any of proposed routes."49 As Commission

Staff asserts, it does not contest the viability of any proposed routes, including those that include

Link F34.

        Despite some intervenors' contention that routes using Link F34 should be disqualified, 50

modifications can be made to address the concern regarding the proximity ofthe school ifLink F34
